children.characters: LUMBOX: B2B Platform for Indonesia’s Agricultural Supply Chain

children.name: Project description
children.characters: Designing an integrated platform for aggregators, smallholder farmers, buyers, and ID FOOD's staff and executives, connecting every layer of Indonesia's agricultural supply chain in one system.

children.name: Overview text
children.characters: Every year, Indonesia loses enough food to feed 125 million people, while farmers capture only a fraction of what it's worth.

children.name: Overview text
children.characters: Lumbox is our submission for Proto-A-Thon International Design Competition 2026, developed for a case study in collaboration with ID FOOD, Indonesia's state-owned food holding company. Here's the problem we uncovered, and the system we designed to solve it.

children.name: Problem description
children.characters: Indonesia's food supply chain loses IDR 551 trillion annually (4-5% of GDP) to inefficiency. Prices markup 7-10x from farmer to consumer, yet farmers capture just 15-20% of that value, leaving 48 million smallholder farmers excluded from formal markets and fair pricing.

children.name: Solution description
children.characters: A platform that formalizes, not eliminates, the informal actors already holding the chain together (tengkulak). Connecting 500,000+ aggregators and 48 million smallholder farmers to verified B2B buyers, tailored across every level of the organization, from field collectors to ID FOOD's staff and executives.

children.name: Problem description
children.characters: To understand why the system was breaking, we started by mapping where the money and the food were actually going.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.characters: Lost annually 4–5% of GDP, exceeding the entire Ministry of Agriculture budget.

children.name: Metric 2 description
children.characters: Average distribution time for fresh produce, against a 1–3 day shelf life.

children.name: Metric 3 description
children.characters: Price markup from farmer to consumer while farmers capture only 15–20%.

children.name: Metric 4 description
children.characters: Smallholder farmers still excluded from formal markets and digital systems.

children.name: Problem summary
children.characters: The crisis is not a lack of harvest, capital, or ambition, it is the absence of a unifying layer that connects what already exists

children.name: Goals text
children.characters: The future of Indonesia’s food supply chain is not built by removing intermediaries entirely, but by formalizing and orchestrating their essential functions into a transparent, tech-enabled ecosystem

children.name: Goals text
children.characters: Here’s what we’re committing to build:

children.name: Goals summary
children.characters: Rather than disrupting the actors already holding this chain together (informal aggregators/tengkulak), we set out to formalize and orchestrate them, building a system where every role becomes more valuable, not obsolete.

children.name: HMW intro text
children.characters: After interviewing farmers and middlemen across the supply chain and analyzing where the system breaks down, we distilled everything into one core question:

children.name: HMW question text
children.characters: “How might we create a more transparent, connected, and efficient food supply chain ecosystem that helps farmers, middlemen, and businesses access fair pricing, smarter distribution, reliable logistics, and data-driven decision making while reducing food waste and market uncertainty?”

children.name: Solution intro
children.characters: With that question in mind, we looked at why past agritech solutions had failed and realized most of them tried to eliminate the very actors, like tengkulak (middlemen), who were quietly holding the chain together. So instead of removing them, we designed a system to formalize what they already do.

children.name: Products description
children.characters: Three surfaces. One ecosystem. Every actor in chain, from the farmer who grows it, to the collector who moves it, to the business that needs it, finally connected

children.name: Feature 1 title
children.characters: TRANSPARENT FARM PRODUCTS COLLECTION & CONNECTIVITY THROUGH LUMBOX CONNECT

children.name: Feature 1 description
children.characters: The collector negotiates with the farmer on-site and inputs the transaction details into the app: Farmer’s Name/NIK, Commodity, Volume, Agreed Price/kg, and Payment Method (Cash or Cashless via Bank Account). To finalize the purchase, the collector must trigger an automated summary sent directly to the farmer’s WhatsApp/SMS. This forces a transparent, honest ledger where the offered price is benchmarked against real-time market data.

Conclusion text
children.characters: By activating ID FOOD's existing infrastructure, Lumbox aims to transform informal networks into a connected digital ecosystem, shifting national food governance from reactive monitoring to real-time orchestration.

children.name: Conclusion summary
children.characters: From scatterd harvest to a connected nation, built chain by GRAIN.

children.name: Project title
children.characters: Evaluating the Robustness of Classical Machine Learning in Cross-Subject EEG Seizure Detection

children.name: Project description
children.characters: A classical ML pipeline trained on 3.5M+ EEG windows to test whether seizure detection still works on patients the model has never seen. Presented at BIOXPLORE 2026 (IEEE & Scopus-indexed).

children.name: Type value
children.characters: Research Paper / Machine Learning Study, IEEE Conference

children.name: Team value
children.characters:
Daffa Farras Putra Tarigan
Kevin Fransisco
Aqila Ananti
Muhammad Zick Al-Farizi
Nadya Syifa Azzahra

children.name: Result value
children.characters: Presented at BIOXPLORE 2026 (IEEE Conference No. 68070X, Bantul, 5 August 2026). Indexed by IEEE & Scopus.

children.name: Overview text
children.characters: Epilepsy affects millions of people, and EEG interpretation still depends on specialists reviewing recordings by hand, which is slow and hard to scale. Many published models report near-perfect accuracy, but they are often tested on data from the same patients they trained on.

children.name: Overview text
children.characters: This project is our research submission to BIOXPLORE 2026. We ask a harder question: how well do classical machine learning models work on completely unseen patients?

children.name: Problem description
children.characters: Seizure windows make up only 0.067% of the data, and every patient's brain signals look different. Under these conditions, accuracy and ROC-AUC can make a useless model look excellent.

children.name: Solution description
children.characters: We built a strict, leak-free evaluation pipeline. It combines subject-wise splitting, Leave-One-Subject-Out validation, and AUC-PR as the primary metric. We used it to benchmark four classical models under realistic deployment conditions. We did not propose a new algorithm. Instead, we provide an honest empirical baseline.

children.name: Problem description
children.characters: To see why seizure detection breaks in practice, we looked at the CHB-MIT scalp EEG data and measured how hard the task is.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.characters: two-second EEG windows from the CHB-MIT database (23 cases, 198 annotated seizures).

children.name: Metric 2 description
children.characters: only 2,365 windows are seizures, against 3,535,516 non-seizure windows.

children.name: Metric 3 description
children.characters: extracted per window (77 zero-variance features were removed afterward).

children.name: Metric 4 description
children.characters: train and test sets contain different patients (2,768,685 train and 769,196 test windows).

children.name: Problem summary
children.characters: The crisis is not a lack of harvest, capital, or ambition, it is the absence of a unifying layer that connects what already exists

children.name: Problem description
children.characters: Three things make this task difficult:

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.characters: A model that always predicts "no seizure" is right 99.9% of the time.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.characters: Different patients produce different EEG patterns, so a model that works on one patient often fails on another.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.characters: High accuracy or ROC-AUC does not mean good seizure detection.

children.name: Problem summary
children.characters: The problem is not a lack of models or accuracy scores. It is the lack of evaluation that reflects real clinical conditions.

children.name: Problem summary
children.characters: The heatmap shows near-zero linear correlation with the label and strong multicollinearity between neighboring electrodes, which is expected because of volume conduction.

children.name: Goals text
children.characters: Reliable seizure detection needs honest evaluation before it needs a bigger model. We set out to test three hypotheses:

children.name: Goals text
children.characters:
No significant performance difference exists among classical models for cross-subject detection.
Severe class imbalance degrades detection performance.
Accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating seizure detection.

children.name: Goals text
children.characters:
A reliable baseline for future patient-independent EEG research.
Evidence that clinically meaningful metrics should replace accuracy-only reporting.
Guidance on models that fit initial clinical screening, where missed seizures cost more than false alarms.

children.name: Award Title
children.characters: "How well do classical machine learning models generalize to completely unseen patients under extreme class imbalance and inter-subject variability?"

children.name: Goals text
children.characters: Instead of building a new detector, we built a realistic test bench in six steps.

children.name: Products description
children.characters: Raw EEG was filtered with a zero-phase, 4th-order Butterworth band-pass filter at 0.5–40 Hz. The 0.5 Hz cutoff removes baseline wander and sweat artifacts. The 40 Hz cutoff suppresses muscle noise and interference.

children.name: Products description
children.characters: The signal is cut into 2-second windows with a 1-second step. A window is labeled "seizure" if it overlaps any part of an annotated seizure.

children.characters:
Time domain:
mean, standard deviation, variance, and Shannon entropy. Lower entropy often signals seizure-related hypersynchrony.

Frequency domain:
Welch's power spectral density and band power in Delta (0.5–4 Hz), Theta (4–8 Hz), Alpha (8–13 Hz), and Beta (13–30 Hz).

children.name: Products description
children.characters: Data is split by patient, never by window. Logistic Regression, SVM (RBF), Random Forest, and XGBoost (GPU, Optuna-tuned) were tested. Class weighting and random under-sampling were applied to training data only, to avoid evaluation bias. LOSO validation was run on Logistic Regression, because simple models keep learned weights interpretable.

children.name: Products description
children.characters: ROC curves look strong, but PR curves reveal poor detection of the minority seizure class.

children.name: Goals text
children.characters:
Random Forest and XGBoost: Accuracy is above 0.998, but recall is zero. They collapsed into predicting only "non-seizure".
Logistic Regression: It caught about 75% of seizure windows and has the highest AUC-PR. The cost is roughly 80,000 false positives, which could cause alarm fatigue for neurologists.
Under-sampling: Recall rose (Random Forest reached 0.9395), but precision fell to about 0.003. The SVM's AUC-PR could not be computed (NaN).
Class weighting: Results stayed close to baseline. Logistic Regression again led with an AUC-PR of 0.0278.
XGBoost tuning: Optuna tuning reached an objective score of 0.3353, yet recall was still zero. Model complexity did not fix the problem.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.characters: Realistic evaluation protocol: Strict subject-wise split and LOSO validation to prevent leakage.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.characters: Proper metrics: AUC-PR as the primary metric, to avoid misleading performance claims.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.characters: Practical insight: Simpler models can outperform complex ones under extreme imbalance.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.characters: Repeated trials and statistical significance tests were not run because of limited compute.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.characters: LOSO was applied only to Logistic Regression.

children.name: Metric 1 description
children.characters: Deep learning was intentionally excluded, to keep the comparison controlled and interpretable.

children.name: Conclusion text
children.characters: Classical ML struggles with cross-subject seizure detection. Accuracy is unreliable for imbalanced medical data, so AUC-PR should be used instead. Future work will explore autoencoder-based anomaly detection, contrastive learning (Siamese networks), Focal Loss with hard example mining, and repeated LOSO runs with non-parametric significance tests.

children.name: Icon 1 label
children.characters: Honest Evaluation: Patient-independent validation, not inflated scores.

children.name: Icon 1 label
children.characters: Right Metrics: AUC-PR over accuracy for clinical relevance.

children.name: Icon 3 label
children.characters: Next Step: Representation learning and anomaly detection.

children.name: Conclusion summary
children.characters: "High accuracy is not detection. Measuring honestly is the first step to saving lives."
